extracted.intended_audience: writers, students, and readers learning narrative point of view
extracted.subtask_description: A concise guide to identifying and using first-, second-, and third-person narrative points of view, including the three third-person subtypes (omniscient, limited, objective), with examples and notes on effects and limitations. Useful for writers deciding how to frame a story and for students learning narrative technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification by pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Narratives are often identified as first, second, or third person based on the kinds of pronouns they utilize: first-person uses I or we, second-person uses you, and third-person will use he, she, it or they.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The main points of view are first-person and third-person; these types of narrative make up the overwhelming majority of texts you will read. Second-person appears far less frequently, although it is often studied in writing classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Person Point of View
rubrics_metrics.description: In first-person narration, the narrator is a person in the story, telling the story from their own point of view. The narration usually utilizes the pronoun I (or we, if the narrator is speaking as part of a group).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The character who tells the story might be in the middle of the action or more of a character who observes the action from the outer limits, but in either case you are getting that character’s recounting of what happens. Impressions and descriptions are colored by that character’s opinions, mood, past experiences, or even their warped perceptions of what they see and hear. You are likewise shielded from information that the narrator doesn’t know. Example: Jane Eyre (Charlotte Brontë) and other classic first-person voices (The Catcher in the Rye, The Handmaid's Tale, To Kill a Mockingbird). In some stories the first-person narrator may act as an observer of events centered on another character (e.g., Nick Carraway in The Great Gatsby).

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Person Point of View
rubrics_metrics.description: Second-person narration is a technique in which the action is driven by a character ascribed to the reader, one known as you. The narrator describes what 'you' do and lets you into your own thoughts and background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reader is immersed into the narrative as a character involved in the story; allowing the reader to 'be' the central character provides an immersive reading experience and can enhance what is at stake for the character and reader. Second-person is less common in literature but appears in works like Bright Lights, Big City (Jay McInerney) and in 'Choose Your Own Adventure' books for younger readers. Example excerpt from Bright Lights, Big City illustrates addressing the reader directly ('At the subway station you wait fifteen minutes...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Third Person Point of View (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: In third-person narration, the narrator exists outside the events of the story, and relates the actions of the characters by referring to their names or by the third-person pronouns he, she, or they.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third-person narration can be further classified into several types (omniscient, limited, objective). The narrator does not exist as a character in the story and the characters do not acknowledge the narrator’s presence; however, different third-person subtypes vary in the narrator's access to characters' thoughts and knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third Person Omniscient
rubrics_metrics.description: Omniscient means 'all-knowing,' and an omniscient narrator knows every character’s thoughts, feelings, and motivations even if that character doesn’t reveal any of those things to the other characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator is not told through a character but observes all characters and can report their inner thoughts. Example: Little Women (Louisa May Alcott) — the narrator knows what each sister is thinking and can relay those silent thoughts to the reader, showing knowledge beyond any single character's awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third Person Limited
rubrics_metrics.description: In third-person limited narration, the narrator still exists outside the events of the story, but does not know the motivations or thoughts of all the characters. Rather, one character is the driver of the story, and the reader is given a closer peek into that character’s psyche than the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reader is allowed into the focal character's thoughts and impressions while remaining uncertain about what other characters are thinking. Example: the Harry Potter novels use third-person limited with a focus on Harry, giving access to his internal questions and worries but not the private thoughts of other characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third Person Objective
rubrics_metrics.description: In third-person objective narration, the narrator reports the events that take place without knowing the motivations or thoughts of any of the characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator's tone is often matter-of-fact, not colored by opinions or commentary, nor aware of events outside the scene; readers learn about characters through speech and observable actions rather than internal exposition. Example: Shirley Jackson's 'The Lottery' illustrates an objective, reportorial approach where we know little about characters' inner motivations until revealed through dialogue or acts.
